title: Flu arrives early: CDC reports first pediatric death of the 2026-27 season

content:
Flu season is arriving early in the United States, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's October 30 weekly report carries a sobering first for the 2026-27 season: a pediatric death.

The child died during the week ending October 10, and the death was reported later, after investigation, according to reporting on the CDC's FluView update for the week ending October 24. A second pediatric death in the same update belonged to the preceding 2025-26 season, from September — a reminder that a report's publication date is not the date a person became ill or died.

The CDC said early-season influenza activity is currently higher than typically observed at this time of year, while national activity remains low. In the week ending October 17, 99% of influenza A viruses subtyped by public health laboratories were H1N1.

Hospitalizations are also running high for this early in the season. For the week ending October 17, the CDC reported 798 laboratory-confirmed flu-associated hospitalizations, a weekly rate of 1.1 per 100,000 people — and after accounting for reporting delays, an estimated weekly rate of 1.5 to 2.0 per 100,000, the highest weekly rate since the 2010-11 season, according to reporting on the CDC data. The cumulative hospitalization rate was 2.1 per 100,000, more than 10 times the rate observed during the same period last year.

The newer week ending October 24 showed a FluSurv-NET observed weekly hospitalization rate of 1.3 per 100,000, with a delay-adjusted range of 1.9 to 2.5 per 100,000. Those are surveillance estimates, not a final, complete count of admissions nationwide.

In its fall and winter respiratory outlook, the CDC expects a moderately severe flu season across all age groups, with combined hospitalizations from COVID-19, flu and RSV landing close to last season's peak, plus or minus 20%. The CDC recommends an annual flu vaccine for people aged six months and older, with rare exceptions, especially those at higher risk. This story reports the CDC's guidance; it is not medical advice for any individual reader.

What this means locally is still unfolding: an early rise does not necessarily produce a higher seasonal peak, the CDC cautions. Webb Watch 956 will keep following the weekly FluView updates and any Texas Department of State Health Services figures as the season develops.

Sources:

  • NewsCubby, "Flu is rising unusually early: the CDC's latest report explained," October 31, 2026 (reporting CDC FluView, week ending October 24)
  • EIN Presswire, "Flu hospitalization rate reaches highest weekly level since 2010 season," October 31, 2026 (reporting CDC data, week ending October 17)
  • CDC, "Respiratory Disease Season Outlook," October 29, 2026
